name: Teams Formation
description: This time, the Berland Team Olympiad in Informatics is held in a remote city that can only be reached by one small bus. The bus has $$$n$$$ passenger seats, seat $$$i$$$ can be occupied only by a participant from the city $$$a_i$$$. Today, the bus has completed $$$m$$$ trips, each time bringing $$$n$$$ participants. The participants were then aligned in one line in the order they arrived, with people from the same bus standing in the order of their seats (i. e. if we write down the cities where the participants came from, we get the sequence $$$a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$$$ repeated $$$m$$$ times). After that some teams were formed, each consisting of $$$k$$$ participants from the same city standing next to each other in the line. Once formed, teams left the line. The teams were formed until there were no $$$k$$$ neighboring participants from the same city. Help the organizers determine how many participants are left in the line after that process ended. We can prove that answer doesn't depend on the order in which teams were selected.
input_specification: The first line contains three integers $$$n, k$$$ and $$$m$$$ ($$$1 \le n \le 10^5$$$, $$$2 \le k \le 10^9$$$, $$$1 \le m \le 10^9$$$). The second line contains $$$n$$$ integers $$$a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$$$ ($$$1 \le a_i \le 10^5$$$), where $$$a_i$$$ is the index of city where the person occupying the $$$i$$$-th seat in the bus must be from.
output_specification: Output the number of remaining participants in the line.
approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 878B — Teams Formation [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
